title: A learned ODE can be too stiff to integrate and too wrong to time an ignition: diagnostics to plot beside the loss
summary: Five SciML figures look at a learned model of ignition from the outside: how stiff its own Jacobian becomes during training, how its predicted ignition delay compares with the reference, a timing proxy against initial temperature, and the first attempt whose smooth loss curve hid a failed prediction.

media.alt: A yellow line chart titled learned ODE stiffness ratio: epoch from 0 to 2800 on the horizontal axis, stiffness ratio on a log axis from 10 squared to 10 to the sixth, a dashed red reference line at 10 cubed. The curve climbs unevenly, crossing the reference several times, peaks near epoch 2400 and then drops back.

source.caption: Stiffness evolution during training
source.note: DISCLOSURE: figures contain internal model labels (operator, NODE) and run-specific numbers (stiffness ratio at a final epoch, delays). Only the generic reading is taught; no specific values are quoted. The first-attempt figure carries a fuel name in its title, which is not repeated here.
group: 06_neural_ode_results: Where it started — first Neural ODE attempt

read_the_figure.question: Is the learned model getting stiffer than the physics it must reproduce, and does it still get the timing of ignition right?
read_the_figure.axes: Stiffness figure: training epoch against the ratio |lambda_max| / |lambda_min| of the learned Jacobian (log). Delay figures: reference ignition delay (horizontal, microseconds) against predicted (vertical), train and test marked differently, with the dashed line y = x. Timing proxy: initial temperature T0 (1000 to 1600 K) against the progress variable at the peak of OH, reference (dots) and model (squares). First-attempt figure: panels (a) loss, (b) stiffness ratio, (c) OH against time for several T0.
look_at: Stiffness curve against the red threshold line: points above it mean the learned system is stiffer than the usual rule-of-thumb threshold of one thousand. Large swings between checkpoints show the learned model's stiffness is not controlled by the loss.

Delay parity plot: points on the dashed diagonal are perfect. Points on the bottom axis (predicted delay of zero) most plausibly mean no ignition was detected in the prediction; points far above the diagonal are predictions that are much too late.

Timing proxy against T0: reference and model dots should lie on top of each other. Squares stacked at the ceiling at low T0 and reference dots at zero show regions where the two disagree about whether ignition happens at all.

First-attempt figure: panel (a) shows a smooth, steadily falling loss; panel (b) a stiffness ratio in the millions; panel (c) the model's OH (dashed) rising as a straight ramp while the reference (solid) jumps sharply and levels. A smooth loss curve coexists with a qualitatively wrong trajectory.
The two similar timing-proxy stills show the same comparison at two settings; compare them side by side.
read_the_figure.proves: A decreasing loss is not evidence of a correct trajectory: only a rollout against the reference shows timing and shape. A stiffness ratio far above the problem's own tells you integration cost and stability of the learned model, independent of its accuracy.
if_wrong: Ignition-delay points on the bottom axis: the metric returned a sentinel (no ignition); do not average them with real delays.
A smooth loss with a straight-line trajectory: the model learned the mean, not the dynamics.
A stiffness ratio that keeps rising with training: the learned Jacobian is developing very fast modes; expect a stiff solver to be needed.
A train point far off the diagonal while test points sit at the bottom: both failures; judge each split separately.
must_check: That the delay definition is stated (for example time of maximum temperature gradient).
That failures (no ignition) are drawn distinctly rather than averaged.
That a rollout against the reference accompanies every loss curve.
That the stiffness ratio is measured on the learned Jacobian along trajectories, with the threshold stated.

terms.meaning: Time from the initial state to the sharp rise of temperature (or a radical such as OH); defined by a stated rule.
Predicted against reference values; the line y = x is perfect agreement.
Largest to smallest magnitude of the Jacobian's eigenvalues.
The matrix of derivatives of the learned right-hand side, evaluated along a trajectory.
A single number from 0 to 1 that tracks how far a reaction has progressed.
Integrating the learned ODE forward from the initial condition and comparing with the reference.

remember: Loss measures a fit on the training windows; a rollout measures dynamics.
A stiffness ratio above 1e3 usually calls for an implicit solver.
Ignition delay depends sharply on temperature, roughly as exp(E / (R T)).
A parity plot needs the same axes range, a diagonal, and a separate marker for train and test.
Sentinel values (0, NaN) must be shown as failures, not as numbers.

steps.title: Stiffness ratio from the Jacobian
steps.note: The ratio of the fastest to the slowest decay rate of the local linearization. The figures plot it against epoch on a log axis.

steps.title: Cost of integrating a stiff model explicitly
steps.note: A ratio of 1e6 means that an explicit solver needs about a million small steps for each slow time scale; an implicit solver does not.

steps.title: Ignition delay from a rule
steps.tex: \tau_\mathrm{ign}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_t\frac{\mathrm dT}{\mathrm dt}\ \ (\text{or the time of the OH peak})
steps.note: Different rules give different delays; a figure must state which one it uses. A prediction with no sharp rise has no maximum to find, which is how a delay of zero or a missing point can appear.

steps.title: Temperature dependence of a delay
steps.note: The standard Arrhenius form: the log of the delay is linear in 1/T0. A model whose delay does not follow this trend over a temperature range has not learned the controlling chemistry.

worked.title: Steps needed at a stiffness ratio of one million
worked.problem: A learned model has |lambda_max| = 2e4 and |lambda_min| = 2e-2 (per unit time). How many RK4 steps cover one slow time scale?
worked.answer: About 360 000 steps, against a few hundred for an implicit method with accuracy-limited steps.

analyze.q: The stiffness curve dips below the threshold at some epochs and rises again. What does that say about using a single checkpoint as a representative of training?
Why can loss decrease smoothly while the OH prediction is a straight ramp?
Where in the delay parity plot would you look to see failures to ignite, and how would you avoid hiding them in an average?

evaluate.q: A colleague reports only the final loss of the first attempt. Which two additional figures would you require?
evaluate.hint: A rollout and the stiffness of the learned model.

evaluate.q: Is a learned model with a stiffness ratio of 1e6 a failure? Argue both ways, using what the reference system's own ratio would be.

create: Design a three-panel monitor for training a learned stiff ODE: loss, stiffness ratio, rollout error at a fixed horizon, with one threshold per panel.
Redraw the delay parity plot so that non-ignition predictions are drawn at a labelled 'no ignition' margin outside the axes.

checks.q: What does the red dashed line at 1e3 mean?
checks.answer: A conventional threshold above which a problem is called stiff and explicit solvers become inefficient.

checks.q: Why is a predicted delay of zero not a small error?
checks.answer: Because it most plausibly marks a prediction with no ignition event detected: the model failed qualitatively, not quantitatively.

checks.q: The loss in the first attempt falls smoothly. Is training working?
checks.hint: What does the third panel show?
checks.answer: Not necessarily: the OH panel shows a straight ramp where the reference jumps sharply, so the model has not captured the dynamics.

checks.q: Name one metric you would add so that a flat or ramp prediction cannot score well.
checks.answer: Error in ignition delay and in peak OH, reported per condition, alongside the loss.
